chapters.title: Chapter 6: After Filing: Refunds, Notices and Fixing Mistakes

lessons.title: Responding to Income Tax Notices and Building a Yearly Filing Routine

body.text: Most notices are the system asking a question, not the department accusing you of a crime. The only response that reliably makes things worse is silence.

children.text: Almost every notice an ordinary taxpayer receives comes from a computer noticing a gap: income in your AIS that is missing from your return, a TDS credit that does not match Form 26AS, a form that cannot hold the income you declared. Each one has a section number, a deadline and a place on the portal to reply. This final lesson shows you how to read them, how to answer, and how to build a year that produces fewer of them.

cells: Intimation after processing
Automatic, after every return is processed
Only if you disagree, as covered in Lesson 1
Defective return notice
Wrong form, missing schedules or inconsistent figures
Usually 15 days from the intimation
Inquiry before assessment
You did not file, or the officer wants documents
As stated in the notice
Scrutiny notice
Your return has been picked for detailed examination
As stated; the notice itself must be issued within three months from the end of the financial year in which you filed
Reassessment
The department believes income escaped assessment in an earlier year
You first get a show cause opportunity; notices run to 3 years, or 5 years where escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more
Demand notice
Tax, interest or penalty payable after an order
Usually 30 days
Refund adjustment intimation
Your refund is about to be set off against an old demand
Respond before the adjustment is made

body.text: Check that the notice is real before you do anything else. Every genuine communication issued since 1 October 2019 carries a Document Identification Number, and one without a DIN is treated as never issued. Use the Authenticate Notice or Order issued by ITD service on the portal, which works even before logging in, and confirm the same item appears under Pending Actions when you log in directly. Real emails come from an incometax.gov.in address. The department never asks for card details, OTPs or a fee to release a refund.

body.title: The Refund That Needs a Fee
body.question: Ajay gets an SMS saying his ₹18,540 refund is approved but held up, with a link to pay a ₹250 processing fee and confirm his account number. What should he do?
options: Pay the ₹250, since the refund amount matches what he expects
Reply asking for the officer name before paying
Ignore the link, log in to the portal directly, and check Pending Actions and the refund status
Forward it to his bank for verification
body.explanation: The department never charges a fee to release a refund and never asks for account details by SMS. Scammers often quote a realistic amount, sometimes picked up from a data leak. The safe move is always the same: type the portal address yourself, log in, and check Pending Actions, e-Proceedings and the refund status. Nothing genuine ever requires a link from a message.

children.text: How to Respond, Step by Step

events.title: Read and Record
events.description: Note the section, the assessment year, the DIN and the deadline. Most panic comes from not reading the first paragraph, which usually states exactly what is wanted.

events.title: Authenticate
events.description: Use the Authenticate Notice service with the DIN and your mobile number, or your PAN and document details.

events.title: Open the Proceeding
events.description: Log in and go to Pending Actions, then e-Proceedings. The notice, the query and the reply window all sit there.

events.title: Gather the Evidence
events.description: Pull the documents that answer the specific question: Form 26AS, AIS, bank statements, broker reports, premium receipts, the rent agreement.

events.title: Submit the Response
events.description: Answer in the portal, attach the documents, and submit before the deadline. Ask for more time through the portal if you genuinely need it.

events.title: Save the Acknowledgement
events.description: Download the acknowledgement of your response and keep it with that year folder, along with the notice itself.

columns.label: Do This
points: Read it fully and identify the exact question
Respond through the portal, within the deadline
Answer only what was asked, with documents that support it
Get professional help for scrutiny, reassessment or large amounts

columns.label: Never Do This
points: Ignore it, or assume it will go away after the refund arrives
Click a payment link in an email or SMS
Pay a demand you believe is wrong without recording your disagreement
File a fresh return when the notice asks for a response to a proceeding
Send documents to an individual email address that asks for them

body.title: The Mark of a Genuine Notice
body.textWithBlank: Every genuine communication from the department issued on or after 1 October 2019 carries a unique ___, and one issued without it is treated as never issued.
body.explanation: The Document Identification Number lets you verify any notice, order, summons or letter through the Authenticate Notice service on the e-filing portal, without even logging in.

body.title: The Defective Return Notice
body.scenario: Rehana, a salaried designer in Mumbai, filed ITR-1 on 22 July 2026. She had sold shares in December 2025 with a short-term gain of ₹90,000, and she simply added it to her other income, because ITR-1 had no obvious place for it. On 3 September 2026 she receives a notice describing her return as defective, giving her 15 days to respond.
body.prompt: What went wrong, what should Rehana do now, and what should she do differently next year?
body.modelAnswer: ITR-1 cannot hold a short-term capital gain at all, so her return was filed on the wrong form, and squeezing the gain into other income also taxed it wrongly: short-term gains on listed shares are taxed at 20%, not at her slab rate. Her first step is to authenticate the notice and open it under Pending Actions, then e-Proceedings, where the department states the defect. She responds within 15 days by filing a corrected return in ITR-2, reporting the gain in Schedule CG, and e-verifying it. If she does nothing, the original return can be treated as never filed, which would leave her with a late return, a late fee and interest. Next year, her routine fixes this before it starts: she downloads her broker tax report in June, sees the capital gain, and picks the form after listing her income rather than before. The wider lesson from this course is that the ITR form is chosen by your most complex income, not your largest.

children.text: The Notice You Can Prevent: AIS Mismatches

The department also runs campaigns that are not formal notices: messages telling you that a high value transaction in your AIS does not appear to match your return. Take Preeti, who redeemed mutual fund units worth ₹6,20,000 during the year and reported a long-term gain of ₹40,000 in her return. Her AIS shows the ₹6,20,000, and the campaign message asks her to confirm. Nothing is wrong: AIS reports sale value, not gain, and her gain is correctly reported. She simply confirms the information is correct in her AIS feedback and keeps her capital gains statement on file. Had she genuinely forgotten the redemption, the right response would be a revised return, which Lesson 2 covered.

body.label: The Habit That Prevents Most Notices
body.context: Once around October, when half the year is visible, and again in June before filing. Almost every routine notice traces back to something that sat in AIS and never reached the return.

children.text: Filing well is not an annual heroic effort in July. It is a handful of small habits spread through the year. Here is the routine for FY 2026-27, the year you are living in now.

events.title: Set Up the Year
events.description: Create a folder for the year. Tell your employer which regime to use for TDS, and declare rent or interest income so salary TDS covers it.

events.title: First Advance Tax Instalment
events.description: Pay 15% if you expect tax above ₹10,000 beyond TDS. Your Form 16 for the previous year also arrives by now.

events.title: File and Verify Last Year
events.description: File by 31 July, or 31 August for non-audit business returns, and e-verify the same day.

events.title: Second Instalment, and a Mid-Year AIS Check
events.description: Pay to 45% cumulative, and reconcile AIS for the first half of the year while the entries are still fresh.

events.title: Third Instalment
events.description: Pay to 75% cumulative. Also the month when the previous year belated window closes on 31 December.

events.title: Close the Year Properly
events.description: Submit investment proofs to HR if you are in the old regime, pay the final instalment by 15 March, and check that your PAN, Aadhaar, bank and nomination details are all current.

events.title: Year Ends
events.description: Download interest certificates and broker statements for the year, and file them in the folder you created in April.

cards.term: Your return was processed and the department agrees
cards.definition: Intimation under Section 143(1), now Section 270(1). Save the PDF as proof.

cards.term: You filed ITR-1 but had capital gains
cards.definition: Defective return notice under Section 139(9), now Section 263(9). Usually 15 days to respond.

cards.term: The officer wants documents, or you never filed
Your return is being examined in detail
cards.definition: Scrutiny notice under Section 143(2), now Section 270(2), issued within three months from the end of the financial year of filing.

cards.term: The department thinks income escaped assessment years ago
cards.definition: Reassessment under Sections 148A and 148, now Sections 281 and 280, with a show cause step first.

cards.term: Tax is payable after an order
cards.definition: Demand notice under Section 156, now Section 289, usually payable within 30 days.

cards.term: Your refund is about to pay off an old demand
cards.definition: Refund adjustment under Section 245, now Section 438, after a prior intimation.

body.title: The Routine, in Seven Habits
steps: Keep one folder per financial year, and drop documents into it as they arrive
Check Form 26AS once a quarter, after each TDS return cycle
Reconcile AIS in October and again in June
Pay advance tax on non-salary income, or have your employer include it in TDS
File early enough to fix surprises, and e-verify immediately
Open every email from the department the day it arrives, and authenticate any notice before acting
Keep PAN, Aadhaar, bank pre-validation, contact details and nominations current

points: Most notices are automated queries about gaps between your return and the department records, and every one has a section, a deadline and a place on the portal to reply
Verify the Document Identification Number through the Authenticate Notice service before responding, and never act on links in emails or SMS
A defective return notice, under Section 139(9) and now Section 263(9), usually gives 15 days, and ignoring it can make the return invalid

Scrutiny notices under Section 143(2), now 270(2), must be issued within three months from the end of the financial year in which you filed; reassessment runs to 3 years, or 5 years where escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more
Respond through Pending Actions and e-Proceedings, answer only what is asked, attach evidence, and keep the acknowledgement
The routine beats the panic: one folder a year, quarterly Form 26AS checks, AIS reconciled twice, advance tax paid on non-salary income, and a return filed and verified early

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Notice types, time limits and portal processes reflect the position at the time of writing and can change. Deadlines depend on the specific communication you receive, and scrutiny, reassessment and penalty proceedings carry consequences that justify professional representation. Verify everything on the Income Tax Department portal or with a qualified tax professional.
